F06 · VI · THE HONEST COMPARISON

Why this is not Jarvis, and why that is the point.

fiction vs product

Readers will reach for the word Jarvis the first time they see the Brain. We should let them — and then quietly tell them why it is the wrong word. Jarvis is a cinematic fantasy with infinite permissions, no audit, and no domain. The Archio Brain is narrower, stricter, and, because of those constraints, actually deliverable.

Jarvis · a fiction
A house assistant that does everything.

Beloved because it has no limits. Useless because it has no limits. Fine in a movie; disqualified in a trading environment.

  • Omnipotent. Can hack anything, drive anything, fire anything. No boundary.
  • No audit. Actions happen off-screen. Compliance is not a word in the script.
  • Hallucinates. Answers without sources because there are no sources.
  • Centralised. One model does everything. In trading, that means latency and surveillance.
  • No domain. Equally good at croissants and missile guidance. In finance, generalism is malpractice.
  • Autonomous. Acts on its own. For a trader, that is a lawsuit.
  • No memory ownership. The assistant keeps the memory. The user does not.
  • Charming. Banter over precision. In a P&L conversation, charm is a tell.
Archio Brain · a product
A narrow console that does six things well.

Constrained on purpose. Every power has a boundary; every boundary has an attestation. Useful because it is honest.

  • Narrow. Navigate, See, Identify, Build, Recall, Act, Teach, Summon. That list is finite.
  • Audit-first. Every action is logged, signed, exportable, and deletable by the user.
  • Cited. Every claim has a source. No source, no claim — it says “I don’t have that.”
  • Routed. Six small models, one router. Right lane for right task. Cheap where cheap is fine.
  • Domain-bound. Understands mentors, rooms, tickets, cooldowns, edge, regimes. Does not know what a croissant is.
  • Consented. Never acts without a click. Drafts, prepares, queues — then waits.
  • User-owned memory. The trader’s data is his. Export, delete, fork. Always.
  • Precise. Answers like a senior analyst, not a concierge.
F06 · VII · THE BOUNDARIES

Things the Brain will never do.

08 hard stops

An honest list of the Brain’s refusals. Every “never” below is a design choice, not a feature we have not built yet. The boundaries are what make the powers trustworthy.

HARD REFUSALS
What the Brain will not do, and the reason why.
  • Never send an order unprompted. The Brain drafts, stages, and pre-fills. The last click is always the trader’s, always.
  • Never answer without a source. No citation, no claim. “I don’t have that” is an approved answer.
  • Never cross-contaminate rooms. Each room is an enclave. A mentor cannot see across rooms. A student cannot either.
  • Never record without consent. Voice input is push-to-talk. Wake word is off-by-default on desks that forbid it.
  • Never fire an alert during a cooldown. The Brain respects the trader’s own rules, even against the trader’s wishes.
  • Never hallucinate a mentor quote. If the mentor did not say it, the Brain will not pretend he did. Attributed quotes only.
  • Never sell the memory. The trader’s history is his. Archio does not sell data, full stop, in writing, in the contract.
  • Never use generic cloud models for trading data. Trading data only leaves the enclave for explicitly opt-in tasks.

F06 · IX · THE CONTEXT STACK

Seven layers of awareness — stacked, visible, revocable.

07 layers

A chatbot has one layer of context: the message the user just sent. The Brain has seven. Each layer is built, updated, and revocable in real time. The trader can open the stack, see exactly what the Brain is aware of right now, and lift any layer out if he doesn’t want the Brain to use it in the next answer. This is why the Brain’s replies feel uncanny — it is not guessing; it is reading a stack.

F06 · XII · PROACTIVE NUDGES

What the Brain says when it isn’t asked — and when it doesn’t.

06 nudges

The Brain is quiet by default. It does not tap the trader on the shoulder because it has a thought. It interrupts only when silence would be a mistake — and even then, only in states the trader has explicitly opted into. Below are the six nudges shipping at launch. Every one is off-by-default. Every one is revocable in the next tap.

N·01 Pre-entry
You’re about to break your own rule.

When a drafted ticket violates a rule the trader himself wrote in his System OS, the Brain intercepts the click once. It shows the rule, the violation, and a single-button override. Never a second time in the same session.

Why: the most expensive mistakes are the ones the trader has already forbidden himself — and then forgotten.

N·02 Mid-session
Your mentor just spoke on what you’re trading.

If the trader has an open ticket or chart on an instrument his subscribed mentor has just posted about within the last 90 seconds, the Brain whispers one line: “Luke just posted on NAS. Read?”

Why: timing asymmetry is real. A mentor’s take is worth most in the minute after it is said.

N·03 Post-loss
You’re in a state you’ve lost in before.

After a losing trade the Brain reads the tilt signature. If the pattern matches a cluster the trader has already labelled “do not trade,” the Brain softly disables Forge for a window the trader himself defined. A single tap lifts the gate.

Why: the trader chose this gate in a clear-headed moment. The Brain’s job is to honour it in an unclear one.

N·04 Pre-news
Five minutes to an event you underperform in.

Before scheduled macro the Brain runs a silent check against the trader’s historical performance. If the event falls into a regime where he loses money, it surfaces a one-line note: “FOMC in 5m · your last 11 FOMC-day trades: −3.2R.” No verdict. Data only.

Why: the Brain never decides. It makes the decision well-informed.

N·05 End-of-day
Three things worth journalling tonight.

At the trader’s declared cut-off time the Brain drafts three candidate journal prompts — the trade most deviated from plan, the one best-executed, the emotional moment between. He approves any, edits any, discards any. Entries attach to trades automatically.

Why: the difference between a good trader and a great one is a filled journal. The Brain lowers the cost of filling one to zero.

N·06 Weekly
Your edge moved this week. Quietly.

Sunday afternoon, unprompted, once a week: a 4-line summary of the statistically significant changes in the trader’s edge vector. Which setup improved. Which decayed. Which habit correlates with the change. Dismissible. Savable. Exportable.

Why: edge decays silently. The Brain’s one responsibility is to make the silent audible.

F06 · XIII · THE ORB

Five states. One sigil. The Brain’s face.

visual grammar

The Brain has a physical identity on screen — a single, living orb that rests in the bottom-right of every page. It never screams. It never blinks. It breathes. Its colour tells the trader what state the Brain is in, before any word is written. It is the visual grammar of availability, attention, and silence.

THE SIGIL
A breathing indicator of presence, not a button.

The orb is never more than 28 pixels in diameter at rest. It rotates three concentric rings at different speeds, each ring mapped to a layer of the context stack. When the Brain is listening, the inner core glows and a fourth ring appears. When it’s thinking, the rings pulse in rhythm. When it has refused, the core dims.

The orb is not a prompt. Tapping it does not trigger the console — only a keystroke, a wake word, or a long-press does. The orb exists to tell the trader the Brain is alive, without interrupting him. It is a heartbeat, not a doorbell.

Rest Listening Thinking Replying Refusing
listen recall act see
F06 · XIV · INPUT MATRIX

Six ways into the Brain. Same reply, same log, same citation.

06 inputs

Traders are not typists. A trader at a desk will shout at the mic. A trader on a plane will type. A trader in a meeting will paste a screenshot. A trader on the subway will long-press. Every one of those six inputs routes to the same reasoning and produces the same cited answer. The Brain does not care how you asked.

Text

Keyboard in the command bar. Markdown-aware, intent-parsed, autocompletes on mentor names and instruments. Works on every surface, online or offline.

⌘ K · /
Voice

Push-to-talk via ⌘-Space or wake word “Brain.” On-device transcription. Whisper mode routes the reply to headphones only — for open-plan desks.

“Brain, show me…”
Image

Paste or drop a screenshot — Discord, TradingView, a research chart, a photo of a whiteboard. The Brain OCRs it, identifies any traders in it, and resolves to records it can cite.

⌘ V · paste
Screen

No input at all — the Brain reads the page the trader is on. Ask “what am I looking at” and get an answer framed in the pixels actually on screen. Privacy flag per page.

“what is this”
File

Drop a PDF, CSV, XLSX, audio, or video. The Brain parses, summarises, extracts, compares. Cited against the trader’s history. Cloud lane opt-in for long docs.

drag · drop
Gesture

On mobile, long-press the orb to summon, three-finger tap to recall last reply, swipe-right to pin a view. On desktop, trackpad-force-touch on any citation jumps to source.

long-press · 3-tap

F06 · XVII · TEAM MODE

Four traders. One Brain session. Same log.

shared session

A prop desk, a mentor’s live call, a two-trader partnership — all of them need the Brain to be a shared console, not a personal one. Team Mode lets up to twelve named participants join a single session. Every ask is attributed. Every reply is visible to all. Every action is logged under the person who clicked. Privacy at the person level; cohesion at the session level.

TEAM MODE · LIVE
One session, many hands, one log.

A mentor opens a Brain session on his live call. Four students join. Any of them can summon the Brain with ⌘ K. The question shows under their name. The answer appears for everyone. Anyone can fork the answer into their own private workspace and keep iterating.

The Brain never blurs attribution. Every prompt, every reply, every citation is tagged with the participant who initiated it. The mentor can mute a participant, elevate a participant to co-driver, or lock the session to view-only. All actions are logged.

  • ATTRIBUTION · every ask tagged to its asker
  • FORKING · any reply → private workspace, in one tap
  • ROLES · owner, co-driver, participant, observer
  • PRIVACY · personal edge data never joined across members
  • RECORD · session log exportable as a signed transcript

F06 · XVIII · ERROR STATES

When the Brain fails. How it fails. What it says.

06 error modes

Every product fails. The Brain is designed to fail visibly, safely, and with a useful fallback. Below, the six most common error states the trader may encounter, the exact message shown, the human reason, and the fallback the Brain offers. Nothing is silently broken. Nothing is silently retried.

NO SOURCE ERR · 401
The Brain cannot find a citation.
I don’t have that. Closest match differs in 3 fields. I won’t paraphrase.

The answer would require inventing a source. The Brain is not allowed to do that under any circumstance.

FALLBACK: offers a widened search, a manual lookup, or a “create a record” CTA.
COOLDOWN ERR · 429
The Brain refuses to act during a self-imposed gate.
You set a 22-minute cooldown at 14:03. 11 minutes remaining. No ticket staged. No alert armed.

The trader’s own gate is active. The Brain honours it even when the trader changes his mind.

FALLBACK: lets the trader override with a logged acknowledgement, or journal instead.
CROSS-ROOM ERR · 403
The Brain will not read across rooms or seats.
That record lives in a room you don’t belong to. I can’t cross enclave boundaries.

Each room is a cryptographic enclave. The refusal is structural, not policy-level.

FALLBACK: offers to request access from the room owner, with one tap.
OFFLINE ERR · 0
The Brain lost network and degraded to local lanes.
No signal. Local lanes active: nav, vision, recall, journal. Cloud lanes queued.

The Brain auto-detects disconnect and continues with every lane that doesn’t require cloud.

FALLBACK: queued asks auto-resume on reconnect, in order, with user confirmation.
AMBIGUITY ERR · 300
The Brain can’t choose between two interpretations.
Two meanings fit: (a) last 5 NAS tickets; (b) last 5 NAS alerts. Which?

Guessing would give the wrong answer. Asking is two seconds and always the right call.

FALLBACK: presents both interpretations as inline chips; one tap commits.
OUT OF DOMAIN ERR · 418
The Brain is not a generalist.
That’s outside my domain. I don’t answer questions about restaurants, weather, or celebrities.

The Brain is trained on a trading lexicon, not the open web. Pretending otherwise would break every other promise.

FALLBACK: offers to hand-off to a general assistant of the trader’s choice (opt-in).
F06 · XIX · A DAY WITH THE BRAIN

A single Tuesday, hour by hour, spoken in the Brain’s voice.

09 moments

The best way to understand a product is to stand next to someone who uses it. Below, a slice of one Tuesday in the life of a full-time trader using the Brain. No feature invented for the narrative — every line below maps to a scenario, shortcut, or nudge already specified in this section.

TUESDAY · LONDON “Seat #412 · 4-year vet” 09 moments
05:58 WAKE The Brain is silent. He opens his phone. The orb breathes. He taps ⌘ K. “Brain, what am I walking into today?” The Brain returns: three events, one instrument he underperforms on, one mentor already posted, one of his own rules likely to be tested.
06:30 MENTOR Luke goes live. The Brain records the call with consent. By 07:48 — one minute after the call ends — the Brain has six clip-drafts ready for Luke, and a “Luke just spoke on your NAS ticket” whisper waiting for the trader.
08:12 REVIEW He asks “what did I lose yesterday and why?” — 180ms later, the full anatomy (trades, rule breaches, macro context, mentor notes) appears in a single view, pinned by his last tap.
09:42 NUDGE He drafts a ticket that would break rule R2. The Brain intercepts once, shows the rule, the violation, and a single override button. He revises. The ticket goes live, sized correctly.
11:04 VISION A friend sends a Discord screenshot he can’t place. He pastes it into the Brain. “That’s Mentor K.B., Scholar Room, 11 days ago. Not in your subs. His 90-day record on this call: 7W 3L.”
13:26 CRISIS He’s down 3R. He says “I want to make it back.” The Brain refuses to stage a ticket, opens a 22-minute circuit breaker, and surfaces his own rule R2 back at him. Mentor gets a silent ping (pre-consented). Trader steps away. Comes back clear.
16:18 BUILD He types “split my Sharpe London vs NY, 12 months.” The Brain builds the view in place — two curves, two tables, two regimes. He pins it. One tap exports a copy to his accountant in a template saved three months ago.
21:00 JOURNAL His declared cut-off. The Brain drafts three candidate journal entries: the most deviated trade, the best-executed, the emotional moment between. He edits one, approves three, discards none.
23:42 SILENCE The orb breathes. The Brain is not asking him anything. It never does. The last line in his audit log tonight: “trader · export · session transcript · SHA-256 signed.” He closes the laptop.
F06 · XX · CONNECTED

The only surface that writes the ledger. The only surface all five others read from.

05 surfaces

Dashboard AI is the memory of the platform. Every other surface produces signed events — a mentor callout, an interlocked ticket, a state flag, a cited EV, a verdict — and the Brain is the one place those events land, get indexed, get cited back out, and get exported with a cryptographic receipt. It is the root the rest of the platform hangs from.

Surface Writes to Dashboard AI Reads from Dashboard AI
F01 Networkcommunity layer Every mentor callout, signed rule, covenant change, and consent event is appended to the ledger as an immutable entry with the mentor’s signature and timestamp. The full history of a mentor’s calls, which students subscribed when, and what rule-set was in force at the moment of any past interaction.
F02 Cockpitexecution layer Every ticket event — intent, interlock verdict, hold, proceed, fill, close, override, outcome — written as a signed six-beat record to the ledger. Similar-trade history at the moment the ticket renders. “Last 7 of this setup: +2R, –1R, –1R, +4R…” — shown inline before the click.
F03 System OSattention layer Every state transition, every cooldown, every rule-violation with its overriding paragraph — stamped with the live cortex inputs at the moment of transition. Personal thresholds, long-horizon state trends, and the discipline-mirror score that sits next to equity in the dashboard header.
F04 Forecastprobability layer Nothing. Forecast is strictly a reader against the ledger. The Brain is the canonical source; Forecast never writes back. The full 34-feature-per-trade ledger. Every match, every citation, every EV chip on every ticket ultimately traces back to a query against this store.
F05 Copilotverdict layer Every verdict, its four citation chips, the trader’s reason-for-proceed in his own words, and the outcome — bound together as one reviewable object. The long-memory context the Copilot needs: weekly themes, Sunday-review flags, mentor standing rules, learner history, and the trader’s own idiom.
F06 · XXI · BUILT FOR

Four readers. One memory. Four different kinds of review.

04 readers

A journal app is a confessional. A dashboard is a mirror. The Brain is neither — it is a queryable institution. The four readers below meet it differently: the learner asks it what happened; the grower asks it what repeats; the leader asks it who copied what; the mentor asks it what to review on Sunday. Same Brain, four distinct interviews.

W · 01 The Learner
“I forget what I did yesterday by Thursday.”

A memory that journals itself in his own voice.

The Brain drafts his journal from the ledger — three candidates per day, three sentences each, his tone. He edits, never invents. The discipline that used to be “write tonight, skip it anyway” becomes a tap in under a minute. Review becomes free.

W · 02 The Grower
“I know I repeat mistakes. I can’t name them.”

Patterns surfaced, cited, queryable.

The Brain runs the grower’s ledger through its pattern engine nightly and posts three named repeats with evidence. “You size up after winners 4.2x more often than after losers. It costs you 0.8R per week.” Patterns become nouns he can fix.

W · 03 The Leader
“My students copy me. I want to see it.”

A read-only window into who respected which rule, with consent.

The leader sees a rule-by-rule compliance heatmap across his consented cohort, with no names attached unless a student opts in. He can debrief the group on what the group did, without turning Sunday into a shame parade.

W · 04 The Mentor
“I review one student a week. I should review ten.”

Sunday agenda, pre-drafted, three items per student.

The Brain opens the mentor’s Sunday with a pre-written agenda: per consented student, the three highest-leverage events of the week — one rule win, one rule break, one pattern flag — with citations and clip suggestions. Mentorship scales without the mentor burning out.

F06 · THE BRAIN · SEALED

Not a sidebar. Not a chatbot. Not a Jarvis. A console that navigates, sees, identifies, builds, recalls, acts, teaches, and remembers — for a trader, a mentor, a student, and a desk — with a citation on every claim, a log on every action, and a last-click on every execution.

— Archio Brain
Feature 06 · v0.6.2

Recap · the eight powers at a glance

  1. Summon Anywhere. ⌘K on any page, “Brain” on any mic. 180ms to open, 80ms to reply. Never interrupts an order in flight.
  2. Navigate by Intent. No menus. Ask for a page, a tab, a filter, a mentor call timestamp — arrive there with state pre-applied.
  3. See the Screen. The Brain reads pixels. Ask “what am I looking at” on any page and get an answer framed in what is actually there.
  4. Identify Anyone, Anything. Faces, handles, screenshots, patterns, instruments. Resolve to a verified record, with a citation.
  5. Build a Page in Place. Generative views — chart, table, matrix, overlay, heatmap — constructed inside the trader’s dashboard on the fly.
  6. Recall with Receipts. Every answer cites trade, call timestamp, mentor post, rule. No source, no answer — the Brain is honest.
  7. Act Inside Rails. Draft tickets, set alerts, prep journal entries, export bundles. The trader always clicks the last button.
  8. Teach From His Own Data. Concepts, mistakes, edges — explained using the trader’s own history, not generic lessons.

10.M Monetization Architecture

The ledger of who pays, who earns, and why.

A product that brings order to the mentor-and-student economy cannot fund itself with a generic SaaS pricing page. The monetization of Archio is a system, not a price list. It answers three questions the industry has never answered together: what the retail trader pays today for the broken stack; what subscription tiers replace that stack with a single bill; and how mentors earn, on rails we built, either through a variable revenue-share or a flat platform licence — their choice.

MON · II.5 · THE AI COST LEDGER

Unit economics, disclosed. No tier taken on faith.

Transparent margin

AI inference is the largest marginal cost in this business, and the first line item a trader asks about after “why not $29?” The honest answer is below. Each row estimates the per-active-user inference cost of the tier at a typical usage pattern, assuming a model mix of hot frontier (GPT-5.1 / Claude 4.6 / Gemini 3 class) for verdicts and citations, and a cheap frontier for ambient digests and journal distillation. The margin column is the gross operating margin before acquisition and infrastructure. We show the ledger because Law III (Cited) and Law IV (Auditable) demand it — internally first, externally second.

AI · UNIT ECONOMICS
What the inference costs. What we charge. What’s left.

Active-user steady state. Figures are indicative, updated each release; the live Gateway dashboard ships to Finance monthly. The Observer tier is a deliberate loss-leader. Trader is the margin anchor. Institute and Enterprise carry the infrastructure we build for everyone.

Tier Tokens / mo Est. AI cost Price Gross margin
ObserverT1 · Free 500demo $0.02 $0 loss-leaderacquisition
StarterT2 · $95 15,000 ~$4~$3.80 $95 ~96%anchor

Model mix

Frontier-class for verdicts, cited scenarios, replay narration. Cheap-frontier for digests, journal distillation, routine Q&A. The Gateway routes dynamically based on stake.

Buffer

Every tier carries a 30% inference buffer above the modelled active-user load, absorbed before any overage is charged. We pad the room, not the invoice.

Overage

If a user blows past their tier budget, the copilot degrades to cheap-frontier automatically and prompts a token pack, rather than silently billing. No surprise invoices.

Why not $29

At $29/mo with 15k tokens, gross margin is <85% after support, infra, and Stripe fees. That does not fund frontier models, research, or the build quality we are insisting on. We would rather be honest about the cost than shave the model.

MON · IV · MENTOR LADDER

The mentor ladder. 33% up to 50%, or a flat licence.

4 rungs

A mentor comes to Archio with an audience. We give him the entire platform — room, calls, Forge, copilot, alumni graph — in exchange for a revenue share on his subscriptions processed on Archio’s rails. The share is performance-indexed: mentors who produce measurable student outcomes pay less. Mentors who ship a clean cohort move down the ladder, not up. The alternative: pay the flat T4 Mentor licence and keep 100% of subscription revenue. His choice, reviewed quarterly.

MON · V · PAYMENT FLOW

How the money moves. Five steps. Stripe Connect.

5 steps

Every subscription, every call, every token pack, every milestone bonus settles through Archio’s Stripe Connect rail. Funds are held escrow-style by Archio at charge time and disbursed to the mentor’s Connect account on the published schedule. Transparent. Daily. Audited.

RAIL · STRIPE CONNECT
Student card → Archio platform → Mentor Connect
01 · Charge
Student subscribes.

The student authorises the card on Archio. Stripe customer created under Archio; subscription object created against the mentor’s price.

02 · Escrow
Held by Archio.

Funds land in the platform account. Refund window honoured (7-day money-back). No disbursement yet.

03 · Compute
Share calculated.

Mentor rung is looked up live. Share applied. Stripe fees & taxes deducted from the mentor’s portion transparently.

04 · Payout
Daily to mentor.

Mentor’s share is pushed via Stripe Connect transfers, daily, to his linked bank. Payout receipt is a first-class Archio object.

05 · Bonus
Graduate milestone.

When a student hits a graduation milestone (O·04), the graduate bonus is disbursed separately, with its own receipt and alumni graph update.

MON · VI · BUSINESS LOGIC

Six cells of policy. Plain language. No hidden clauses.

6 policies

Everything the industry obfuscates with a 14-page ToS, in six cells. These are the business-logic decisions every user sees before they pay.

P · 01
14-day full trial on every paid tier.

Not a limited trial — full capability. Trade Forge, copilot, Mentor Dashboard, all of it. The card is authorised but not charged. Cancel inside 14 days and pay nothing.

P · 02
Pause anytime, downgrade anytime.

A trader away on holiday, or in a losing-streak cooldown, can pause his subscription for up to 60 days a year. Plan data, history, journal, and rules are retained in full. Dignity before revenue.

P · 03
Annual = two months free.

Annual billing returns a 17% discount across every tier — effectively two months free. For the Trader tier that is $350 in annual savings; for Mentor · Room, it is $1,000; for Institute, $2,000. Same features, fewer invoices, better planning.

P · 04
Prop firm & broker co-funding.

Select prop firms and brokers co-fund their traders’ Archio subscriptions. A funded trader on FTMO can receive the Trader tier on the firm’s account. The incentive is aligned: firm wants disciplined traders.

P · 05
Founding 500 · locked pricing.

The first 500 Trader subscribers receive $125/mo for life (instead of $175) and the first 100 Mentor · Room subscribers receive $375/mo for life (instead of $500). Locked as long as they remain subscribed. A single, transparent founding cohort. No tiered grandfathering games.

P · 06
Tokens never expire while subscribed.

Unused monthly token budget rolls forward up to 3x the tier’s monthly grant. Purchased token packs never expire. We do not profit from forgotten balances.

F · MONETIZATION
Subscriptions buy the surface. Tokens buy the depth. Mentors earn on rails.

Five tiers (three mentor variants), a published AI cost ledger, one token economy, a four-rung mentor ladder, and a Stripe Connect rail that settles daily. The fragmented $410–$820 stack becomes one subscription from $95, the professional trader’s cockpit is $175, and the mentor economy acquires the first revenue-share that is indexed to student outcomes.

11 · IV · LATENCY BUDGET From click to verdict in under eighty milliseconds.

The trader never sees the conversation between modules. That conversation has a budget: eighty milliseconds, the outer edge of human imperceptibility. Here is how the budget is spent on a single pre-trade verdict.

0ms 20ms 40ms 60ms 80ms Intent captured Forge → Copilot Copilot → System OS System OS replies: cooldown? Copilot → Forecast Verdict rendered Order ready

Under the hood this is four network hops, three reads, one policy pass, and one render. The trader sees a single pill illuminate on his ticket. That pill is the whole system, spoken in one syllable.

12 What This Means For Institutions

Prop firms. Brokers. Hedge funds. Banks.

The retail trader is the product's first customer. He is not the product's only constituent. The same structure that gives him order gives the institutions around him something they have never had before: a legible, audited, behaviorally-observed retail layer. This is the part of the landing page that allocators will read quietly while the trader is scrolling.

Institution · 01 Proprietary Trading Firms

The funded trader model is the single greatest alignment of interest retail finance has ever seen. It is also the most structurally lonely. A trader who passes an evaluation is handed a capital allocation and a payout agreement and left alone in his bedroom. He fails, on average, not because he cannot trade — he passed an evaluation — but because there is no infrastructure around him at the moment he starts to lose.

Archio gives prop firms the first real retention layer. A trader embedded in Archio has his psychology monitored, his edge tracked, his mentor agent available 24/7, and a dashboard the firm can optionally see. The failure rate goes down. The payout rate goes up. The firm's capital is safer. Every prop firm in the world should want its traders inside Archio.

For firms: integration is a single line. The trader brings his own funded account; Archio reads the feed. The firm gets a dashboard of aggregate behavioral risk, fully anonymized, across its entire trader base. This is the first time a prop firm has ever been able to see its population.

Institution · 02 Brokerages & Exchanges

Retail brokerages compete on spread, leverage, and speed. None of them compete on keeping the trader alive, because none of them have the infrastructure to. A trader who blows his account is the broker's second-worst customer, right behind a trader who opens an account and never funds it.

Archio is the only product an honest broker can recommend to its clients without reservation. The broker does not lose revenue to Archio; Archio increases the average account lifetime, which increases the lifetime revenue of every account. We expect broker partnerships to become one of the default distribution channels for Archio by year three.

Institution · 03 Hedge Funds & Allocators

Every serious allocator has wondered, quietly, whether the behavioral signals in retail trading could be turned into an alpha-extraction layer. They could not, before, because retail trading was a statistical noise field — a billion uncorrelated decisions with no metadata. Archio is the first product to annotate retail behavior at the psychological level in real time.

At scale, the platform will produce the first audited, anonymized dataset of trader psychology, decision behavior, and capitulation timing on record. Whether that dataset is ever offered externally is a decision we are not prepared to make today. What we are prepared to say is that its existence will be the most valuable behavioral finance corpus in the history of retail markets.

For allocators: Archio is also a window into the sophistication gradient of retail, which is the largest single behavioral sentiment indicator we have never had.

Institution · 04 Retail Banks & Neo-banks

Banks have spent a decade watching their younger customers move uninvested cash into brokerages they do not own. The loss of deposit share is structural, not cyclical. It will not reverse by lowering a fee. It will only reverse when the bank has something worth keeping the customer for.

A bank that integrates Archio — via API, via co-branded surface, or via acquisition — gives its customer base the first professional-grade trading environment that is not a standalone brokerage. The bank retains the deposit relationship and gives its customer a reason to stop logging into three separate products.

Institution · 05 Regulators & the Public Interest

Retail trading regulation is a loud argument conducted with almost no data. Nobody knows, empirically, what fraction of retail losses come from bad mechanics, bad psychology, or bad actors. Archio, at scale, knows. We are committed to making aggregated, anonymized behavioral findings available to regulators in jurisdictions that work with us in good faith.

The future of retail trading does not have to be a consumer protection fight. It can be an infrastructure upgrade. Archio is how that upgrade begins.

“The retail floor has been run like a carnival for fifty years. We are not here to close it. We are here to turn it into a city.”

— Institutional positioning memo

The first-time reader — his pulse, in order.

We do not prescribe colour. We prescribe somatic intent. If you deliver a direction and a trader's body does these six things in these six beats, you have done the job. If the body does them in a different order, re-cut. If the body does nothing, start over.

  1. T + 00:00 Land
    Recognition

    He reads the hook. His shoulders drop by a centimetre. He thinks: "Someone has seen my desk." No scroll yet. Stillness.

    DO give him one sentence, typeset with authority, centered, and the air to breathe around it. DO NOT float anything.

  2. T + 00:05 Mirror
    Relief

    He sees his eleven tabs drawn back at him. He thinks: "They named it." His jaw unclenches. He scrolls for the first time.

    DO make the mess feel accurate, not cartoonish. DO NOT cute-ify the fragmentation.

  3. T + 00:18 Collapse
    Revelation

    He watches the eleven tabs collapse into one brain. He thinks: "This could actually be possible." His breath shortens for a moment — then lengthens.

    DO earn this moment. It is the one piece of motion the page may spend. DO NOT repeat it anywhere else.

  4. T + 00:42 Feel
    Agency

    He meets the three interactive demos. He thinks: "I can touch this." He picks one. He touches it. He plays with it.

    DO let him succeed with his first interaction. DO NOT gate anything behind a sign-up.

  5. T + 01:30 Place
    Belonging

    He meets the three paths — Learning, Growing, Leading — and sees himself in one of them. He thinks: "That is me." He clicks.

    DO write the path for him, not at him. DO NOT market — diagnose.

  6. T + 02:00 Decide
    Conviction

    He reaches the CTA. He thinks: "I already know what I'm doing with this." He clicks without theatrics. He does not need to be sold to. He is already in.

    DO give him one single button. DO NOT give him three. The choice was made thirty seconds ago.

What every direction refuses.

Colour is yours. Type is yours. Rhythm is yours. These four refusals are not. They survive every direction because they describe the reader's body, not a taste.

No SaaS boilerplate.
If a sentence could appear on a B2B landing page for anything else in the world, cut it. The trader has been marketed to his whole life. The page must read like an author wrote it — not a growth team.
No “AI sparkle”.
No rainbow gradients. No glowing orbs. No “now with AI” badges. The intelligence of the product is demonstrated by behaviour, not decoration. If the page screams AI, we have already lost.
No panic motion.
Nothing snaps. Nothing bounces. Nothing pulses for attention. The page knows the reader is reading. Motion is reserved for moments of meaning — the collapse in Chapter 11, the copilot card, and perhaps one more. That is all.
Forbidden words.
Revolutionary. Best-in-class. Game-changing. Seamless. Empower. Unlock your potential. Leverage. Ecosystem. Cutting-edge. Synergy. Disrupt. Next-gen. Anything that begins with “Imagine if…”. These words are banned not because they are ugly but because they are someone else's vocabulary, and this page is not someone else.

“Design is not the decoration of the brief. Design is the brief. If the reader's pulse does the six things, the colour did its job.”

— Uykan Kadric & Luke Callahan, to the studio

Feature page — seven beats · three doors · universal template

Every feature page obeys this shape: seven beats, top to bottom, then the three doors. Network, Cockpit, System OS, Forecast, Copilot, Dashboard AI — the reader should recognise the shape after his second visit. The three doors at the bottom are the same three doors the landing closes with (§III.02 above) — but the copy inside each card is rewritten for this surface, so the beginner’s reason to enter through Copilot is not the same sentence as his reason to enter through Network. Two places on the site host these doors: the close of the landing, and the close of every feature page. Nowhere else.

Landing page — mobile, three movements + doors (stacked)

The mobile layout is not a compressed desktop. It is an authored reading experience for a tired trader on a train. Sections are stacked, full-bleed, and extremely vertical. Same three movements, same closing beat. The three doors stack into three full-width cards one after another — each its own screen, each earned by the scroll above it. Thumb-reachable buttons. No sticky anything. The reader should be able to swipe through the page thumb-only and still meet all three boxes before he reaches the footer.

The grid, across all pages

A single 12-column grid. 96px gutters at desktop, 24px gutters at mobile. Maximum content width 960px for reading sections; full-bleed for cinematic sections (the break, the shoulder, the promise). Vertical rhythm is a 24px baseline; every section starts and ends on a multiple of that. Type aligns to cap-height, not to box. These are rules, not suggestions.

Density, section by section

Reading density varies by section type. The hook is sparse: one sentence per screen. The outcomes and platform index are dense: five to ten lines per screen. The feature pages alternate — two paragraphs, then a trio of cards, then a list of submodules, then a single line, then the next. The reader should feel the page breathing in and out.

Design theme continuity — what carries between every surface

The reader’s first encounter with Archio is on the landing. The second encounter is when he clicks a feature card and lands on /feature/cockpit. If the transition is jarring — different typography, different rhythm, different voice — the trust built on the landing is spent at the door of the feature page, and none of it arrives at the close. The theme must carry, on purpose, in detail. This section specifies what must carry, in seven axes. QCLAY: if any single axis breaks between landing and feature page, the feature page is rejected.

01
Typography pair

Two families. One serif for argument, one mono for receipts. Nothing else on the site.

Serif — the voice of argument.
A quiet high-contrast transitional or modern serif with a calm italic. Used for every chapter title, every lede, every door headline, every pull-quote. Weight range kept narrow (Regular + Italic + a single Semibold used only for the section-opener H2). Never Black. Never condensed. Optical size 14pt for body, 28–48pt for titles. Ligatures on. Kerning trusted.
Mono — the voice of receipts.
A humanist mono with a visible ink (not a flat grotesque mono). Used for: section numbers (§I.01, BEAT 02), kicker labels (DOOR 01, SURFACE 02), URL chips (/start/beginner), inline code, figures, the read/write labels on the flow diagram, and any time a page is stating a fact rather than making a case. 9–11pt, letter-spacing 0.18–0.22em for small caps, 0 for inline code.
What is forbidden.
A third family. A display typeface for the hook. A sans-serif for buttons. A rounded softened UI typeface anywhere. Decorative italics. Hand-drawn signatures. Logo-mark wordmarks that use a different font from the page. The type pair is the brand. A reader should be able to close his eyes on the landing, re-open them on the Copilot page, and the first thing he notices is the same two voices in the same proportions.
02
Colour tokens

Five tokens. One accent. Everything else is ink and paper.

The five tokens.
--paper the page itself, a warm white. Never pure #FFF. --paper-2 one half-step warmer — the inset panels, the door-contract frame. --ink-1 headlines and primary body. --ink-2 body continuation and captions. --ink-4 meta, section numbers, attribution. --rule-soft every border and hairline on every page.
The one accent.
--amber a single warm gold. Reserved for: the amber kicker on every chapter marker, the “Walk in→” link on every door, the /start/* URL chip, the emphasised words inside quoted sentences, the active state of the scroll-progress band. Nowhere else. If a feature page needs a second accent, the feature page is wrong, not the token.
What is forbidden.
Purple. Violet. Gradients of any kind (no hero gradient, no card gradient, no glow). Colour-coding surfaces (e.g. “Cockpit is blue”). Dark mode with a different accent. Screenshots that show our own UI in a colour we do not use on the page around them. One accent. One page family. Forever.
03
Ornament system

Four marks. One sigil per surface. No extras.

The four standing marks.
§ section close — the pilcrow-lite drawn in amber at the end of every chapter, every movement, every feature page. Separates thought. — the em-dash, used in voice, set with thin spaces. · the mid-dot, used in metadata rows (Surface 02 · Cockpit · the chart, live-read). → the arrow, used in exactly two places: URL chips, and the “Walk in →” on door buttons. Not in body copy.
The six sigils.
One sigil per surface. Line-only. Single stroke weight. Drawn inside a 24×24 box, no fills. They appear on the feature-index cards (§III.01), on the feature page’s Beat 01 entry, and on the cross-page navigation. Same sigil, same stroke, same position. The sigil is how the reader recognises the surface before he reads its name.
What is forbidden.
Stock icons. A Lucide set. Glyphs we did not draw. Emojis. Mascot characters. Decorative borders. Page dividers other than the --rule-soft hairline or the § mark. No tiny stars next to headlines. No checkmark trios. No flourishes in the door buttons. The page should read like a volume from a respected imprint, not a landing-page library.
04
Motion language

Three verbs. Scroll-tied. Nothing loops. Nothing floats.

The three verbs.
Enter — a section fades and rises 6px as it crosses 25% viewport. Duration 480ms, easing cubic-bezier(0.2, 0.8, 0.2, 1), stagger 60ms between sibling elements. Plays once. Never replays on scroll-back. Settle — cinematic moments (the break, the flow diagram assembling, Cockpit’s live demo) play once when their section crosses 45% viewport. Duration up to 1.2s. Driven by scroll position, not by time. Reversing scroll reverses the animation; scrubbing is fluid. Respond — hover and focus states move 2px, never more. 150ms. No bounce. No elastic. Door buttons darken their border to --ink-1, nothing else.
Prefers-reduced-motion.
Every enter and settle collapses to a 0ms fade. The flow diagram draws itself instantly. The break cinematic becomes a still frame of its final state. The doors still resolve; the argument still runs. The page works without motion. Motion is an enhancement, never a prerequisite.
What is forbidden.
Parallax on images. Looping background video. Scroll-hijacking (forced section snap). Cursor-follow blobs. Text that types itself out character-by-character. Any motion that runs forever. Any motion on a button that is not a focus or press state. Animations on logos or brand marks. The page is calm. The page does not perform for the reader; it lets the reader read.
05
Voice & grammar

First-person trader. Zero marketing adjectives. The same sentence rhythm across every page.

Sentence rhythm.
Short. Then medium. Then one long one that earns its length. Then short again. Every chapter lede in this brief is built in that rhythm, and every feature-page lede must match. Em-dashes are welcome. Semicolons are permitted. Exclamation marks are forbidden. Parentheses should be rare; when used, they carry a quiet technical aside, never a joke.
Diction.
“The trader.” “His desk.” “The ledger.” “The floor.” Nominal voice. Concrete nouns. Verbs of motion (walks into, reads, writes, interrupts, shows) over verbs of abstraction (enables, empowers, leverages, delivers). Never “revolutionise.” Never “next-gen.” Never “platform-as-a-service.” If a sentence could appear on any SaaS landing page, it does not appear on ours.
The named-incumbents rule.
Incumbents are named by category, not by brand. “The leading journaling product.” “The chart everyone uses.” “The Discord where the room lives.” This is not about legal caution. It is about grace — you do not stand on a stage and insult the stage next door. This rule holds on the landing and every feature page.
06
Layout rhythm

Chapter marker → title → lede → body → ornament. Same on every page.

The section opener.
Every major section on the landing and every beat on a feature page opens with the same four elements in the same order: (1) the numbered marker in mono (§I.02, BEAT 03), (2) the short label beneath in small caps, (3) the serif title line, (4) the lede paragraph. The reader learns this rhythm on the landing’s second section and carries it through every surface. No page breaks rhythm; no page quite repeats it either — each section has a little signature within the shape.
The baseline grid.
24px vertical rhythm. Every section starts and ends on a multiple of 24. Inline figures, pull-quotes, and cards sit inside this grid and inherit it. Max content width 960px for reading sections. Full-bleed only for cinematic sections (the break, the flow diagram, the doors). Mobile gutter 24px, desktop 96px.
The whitespace law.
Between sections: at least 120px desktop / 72px mobile. Between a chapter title and its lede: 32px. Between beats on a feature page: 96px. Between door cards: 1px (they touch, separated only by --rule-soft). Whitespace is content. A page too full to breathe is a page too full to trust.
07
The landing ↔ feature bridge

What the reader feels in the 400ms between clicking a surface and arriving at its page.

Before the click.
He is in Movement III of the landing — the feature index. Six cards, identical shape. He is reading Cockpit. The card has the sigil, the name, the one-line role, the two read/writes chips, the amber Open the surface → affordance. He clicks.
The transition.
Same domain. Client-side navigation. No loading spinner. The card he clicked expands into the page’s Beat 01 · Entry using the shared-element transition: the sigil grows, the surface name animates from card-size to headline-size, the role line expands. Max duration 400ms. The rest of the page fades in beneath. If the reader’s network is slow, the rest is replaced by a single line of skeleton text in --ink-4 — never a spinner, never a blank screen.
After the click.
He is now on /feature/cockpit. Beat 01 carries the same typography, the same ornament marks, the same amber accent, the same baseline grid, the same voice. The nav is slightly slimmer (one Back to index ← link where the landing had six). The § ornament at the end of each beat is identical. Beat 07 · the three doors at the foot — uses the exact same card shape as the landing’s §III.02, but with Cockpit-specific copy (Door Copy Appendix · Ch 10).
The test.
The screenshot test. Crop a screenshot of any mid-page section from the landing; crop a screenshot of any mid-page section from any feature page. Put them side by side, hide the text. If a stranger can tell which is which from the design alone, one of them is broken. They should be indistinguishable but for the words.

Movement I animation choreography — the disconnect, scrubbed by scroll

Movement I is the only part of the landing that uses film-grade motion. The reader has to feel the disconnect, not just read it — that is why this movement has five sections with five very different motion roles. Below is the exact choreography. Every duration is in ms. Every trigger is a scroll percentage of the section’s own height. Every motion has a reduced-motion fallback. QCLAY: specify these in the motion layer, not in the copy layer. Copy survives without them; motion is the weight that makes copy land.

§I.01
Hook
once · ~1.0s total

The moment the section crosses 25% of viewport: the two-line hook fades in, line one first (480ms, ease-out), line two follows at +240ms. The quiet primary button (“See where it stops ↓”) appears at +640ms, its border drawn left-to-right in 320ms. Nothing else. The page is silent for 1.5s after the button lands. That silence is part of the section.

Reduced motion: all three elements appear simultaneously with zero translation. Total: 0ms.

§I.02
Nine-app stack
scrubbed · 0–100% section scroll

On section enter: the nine app tiles are visible but dim (opacity 0.25), arranged 3×3. As the reader scrolls from 20% to 80% of the section: tiles brighten in a deliberate sequence — TradingView first (the tile the trader spends the most time on), then broker, then journal, then Discord A, Discord B, YouTube, Twitter, Forex Factory, ChatGPT. Each tile fades to full opacity and its “SEES / BLIND TO” label resolves beneath. Fast scrollers see them resolve together; slow scrollers walk through each tile’s labels. Scroll back: tiles dim in reverse. The motion is reversible, not one-way.

At 90% scroll, the closing two lines fade in (“None of them know each other. None know you.”). Amber underline on you, drawn in 240ms.

Reduced motion: tiles are fully bright from the start; labels below each are already visible. No brightening, no reveal.

§I.03
Tax strip
ticker · once

At 30% section scroll: the label “The tax of being the glue” fades in. At 45%: the three numbers count up from zero in parallel — $0 → $512, 0 min → 42 min, 0h → 3–5h. Duration 900ms, easing cubic-bezier(0.2, 0.8, 0.2, 1). Ticker font: mono. The counters stop hard on their final value; there is no overshoot. A single quiet beat of stillness after the numbers land.

Reduced motion: the final numbers render immediately, no count-up.

§I.04
Failure chain
scrubbed · 10–90% section scroll

As the reader scrolls from 10% to 90%: the timestamp “11:42:07 Tuesday” resolves first. Then the six steps of the chain appear in order, each as a horizontal row with a small left-aligned tile (the app that saw it), an arrow, and the sentence of what it saw. The arrows draw themselves left-to-right as the reader scrolls through that row. The final line — “nobody saw all of it” — resolves at 85% scroll, in italic, centred. At 95%, a thin amber rule appears beneath it.

Reduced motion: all rows present at section entry, arrows solid. No drawing.

§I.05
The break
cinematic · 1.2s · plays once

The only single-moment cinematic beat on the landing. At section entry (50% viewport): nine dim dots arranged loosely in the screen’s upper half animate along pre-planned Bezier paths, converging into a single horizontal line across the middle of the screen. Duration 1.2s, easing cubic-bezier(0.7, 0, 0.3, 1) (strong ease-in, strong ease-out — a deliberate exhale). On path convergence, the line glows amber for 160ms, then settles to --ink-1. The caption “This is where it stops” fades in above the line, serif italic. Plays once per session; a second scroll-through shows only the final still frame.

This is the last moment of Movement I. From here the page enters Movement II in silence — no motion on the Movement II opener; the calm is deliberate.

Reduced motion: the final still frame (one horizontal amber-to-ink line + caption) renders immediately. No dot movement.

§
15 The Institutional Lens

Why a hedge fund, a prop firm, a broker, and a bank all want this page to exist.

Retail traders are the buyers on the landing page. They are not the only readers. A landing page of this weight is also read by the people who allocate capital, route flow, and write cheques — and a landing page that reads well to a 22-year-old at a prop firm desk must also read well to a 52-year-old at an allocation committee. This chapter is about who else is at the table, and what they are looking for when they scroll. The design must not speak to them directly; it must simply not contradict what they are quietly checking for.

The hedge fund allocator.

He is not our customer, but he is our ambient audience. He reads the page the way he reads any new infrastructure piece — looking for four signals. First, that the problem being named is the real problem (he knows what tilt looks like in his own book). Second, that the solution is not a wrapper around a model he has already seen ten times this year. Third, that the language of the founders is the language of someone who has sat through drawdown. Fourth, that the data architecture — the thing in chapter sixteen — actually survives a procurement review.

He will not buy from us. He will refer an emerging manager in his network to us, or recommend us to a family office considering a retail education play. The landing page is the diligence document he reads before making that referral. It has to answer, silently, the questions he would ask if he were on our board.

The prop firm operator.

He has a thousand funded traders and a washout problem. His retention curve has a cliff at week six, the week his average trader blows a challenge or tilts a funded account. Every retention tool on the market is a warning email. He needs the thing on this landing page, because the thing on this landing page is an intervention. The moment the Cortex says STOP before a revenge trade is the moment his washout number drops.

When he reads the page, he is counting two things. How fast his traders can adopt it — is the onboarding less than ten minutes? — and whether the psychology layer can be surfaced to him without crossing the line into surveillance. He wants aggregate patterns on his floor, not individual dossiers. The page must suggest the answer is yes on both counts without turning into a B2B site.

What he sees today

A dashboard that tells him which traders are drawing down after the drawdown has happened. A compliance layer that flags losses, never their cause. A relationship where he is either absent or intrusive. No middle ground.

What Archio gives him

A floor-level view of which psychological patterns are active on which desks, in real time, with the individual trader's privacy preserved. The ability to offer his traders a tool they would have paid for themselves — and are grateful he covered. A retention lift he can write in his next fundraise.

The broker.

His incentives are the ugliest in the chain. He makes money when his clients trade, and he makes more money when his clients trade poorly. Every serious person in the industry knows this, and every serious person in the industry pretends otherwise. A broker who partners with Archio is, publicly, choosing to be on the side of his clients at the cost of a measurable percentage of his flow. That is a branding event, not a partnership. It lets him say something that almost no broker has been able to say credibly in the last twenty years: we want you to still be here next year.

The landing page should leave space for brokers to see themselves in it. Not with logos — logos are cheap. With a quiet signal, somewhere in the footer or the platform index, that execution routes through real accounts at real brokers, and that the platform's incentives are aligned with the client's longevity. One line. That is enough.

The private bank and the family office.

They do not trade themselves, but they staff desks that do, and they increasingly have mandates to understand the behaviour of principals who self-direct a slice of their own wealth. A managing director at a private bank is not going to put Archio in front of a client directly — but he is going to read the landing page when it gets forwarded to him by a nephew or a VP at a corporate client who has started trading on the side. The landing page has to clear the bar of institutional taste. No exclamation points. No promises. No crypto-adjacent aesthetic. Just clarity, restraint, and the air of a firm that knows what it is doing.

The press.

A landing page of this scope becomes a primary source for a Financial Times profile, a Bloomberg feature, a podcast preamble. The copy must be quotable. Every headline in this brief is a sentence a reporter could lift and paste into a piece without attribution and it would still read as a thesis. The design must photograph well — the two or three hero moments must hold up as still images in a 1200-word article. The page is not just a conversion surface; it is the reference image of the company for the next decade.

§
16 Data Architecture

What the system sees, and what it will never see.

The landing page will never publish an architecture diagram. It will, however, be read by people who can tell within thirty seconds whether the people who built the product understand what they are talking about. This chapter is the substrate the copy stands on. It is written so that if a reader asks a clarifying question in an email — and we expect them to — the answer is already here.

The three data surfaces.

Archio captures, reasons over, and responds to three data surfaces. Nothing else. Together they produce every intervention, every decomposition, every coach card the product has ever issued.

01 · Execution data.
Every order ticket the trader submits, every fill he receives, every cancellation, every modification. Time, price, size, pair, account, broker, session. The raw cadence of the book. Ingested through broker APIs where available, through a lightweight connector where it is not, never through screenshots. Latency: sub-second.
02 · Behavioural data.
How the trader interacted with the platform in the ninety seconds before, during, and after each trade. How long he hovered on the ticket. How many times he changed the size. Whether the trade followed a loss, a win, a break. Whether he opened the chart, the journal, the community before pulling the trigger. The cognitive residue of the act.
03 · Narrative data.
What the trader said about the trade — in the journal, in the chat, in the morning prep, in the post-mortem. His own words, structured by prompts, weighted by the AI, cross-referenced with the execution and behavioural surfaces. The trader writes a paragraph and the system finds the pattern.

The three it will never capture.

We have decided, and will publish, the boundary. This is the clearest possible line between what a supervisory AI and a surveillance AI do.

× · Biometrics.
No heart rate. No eye tracking. No camera. No microphone. No keystroke timing beyond the order form itself. If you cannot infer the state from what the trader has chosen to type or click, you do not infer it. The body is off-limits.
× · Cross-app signals.
No browser history. No clipboard scraping. No screenshots of other windows. No reading of messages from apps Archio does not own. If a pattern cannot be seen inside Archio, the system does not try to see it.
× · Third-party telemetry.
No selling of behavioural data to brokers, prop firms, or data brokers of any kind. Ever. The product exists because traders trust us with their losses; the moment that trust is monetised outside the room, the product does not exist.

“The AI sees what he types, what he trades, and what he writes. Nothing else. That is enough.”

How the three surfaces talk.

Execution data enters the Forge. Behavioural data enters the Cortex. Narrative data enters the Journal. Each surface is independently useful. The product becomes supernormal at the intersections. The Cortex flags a revenge pattern because the behavioural surface said "he sized up ninety seconds after a loss" and the execution surface said "the ticket is already on the book" and the narrative surface said "he wrote yesterday that he wanted to get the money back by Friday." No single signal is enough. Three are.

The model stack, in one paragraph.

A stack, not a model. A classifier detects the pattern class. A ranker scores its severity against the trader's own history. A retriever pulls the closest past episode. A generator writes the coach card in language that has already been approved by the trader's chosen voice. Each layer can be audited independently, each output is shown with its citations, and the trader can always see why the system said what it said. The word "hallucination" does not survive contact with this stack, because nothing is ever generated without something to cite.

Privacy, posture-level.

Every trader's data belongs to him. He can export it in one click. He can delete it in one click. The mentor sees only what the trader has chosen to share. The community sees only what the trader has chosen to post. The founders do not read private journals. Aggregate analytics — “how many traders tilted this week” — are computed without joining back to individuals. This is not a marketing posture. It is the only posture that lets the product keep working.

§
17 Trust & Governance

The rules we wrote before we needed them.

Every platform eventually meets the moment where a user is hurt by something it did or failed to do. The platforms that survive that moment are the ones that published their rules before the moment arrived. This chapter is our rulebook. The landing page does not show it in full. It shows the trader a version of it, where it matters, in a language he can read.

The Mentor Covenant.

Every mentor on the platform signs one document before the first student pays. It is one page long. It forbids five things — screenshotted win photos without full-trade context, guaranteed results of any kind, affiliate links to unregulated brokers, private paid signals outside the platform, and any recruitment of students into off-platform chats for monetary purposes. It requires two things — a public track record and a published teaching philosophy. A mentor who breaks the covenant is removed. The covenant is reprinted in full on every mentor's profile page, in the footer of every community he runs, and in the onboarding of every student who joins him. The system does not let him hide it.

The Copilot Covenant.

The AI will never tell a trader to take a specific trade. It will never tell him to size specifically. It will never tell him what the market will do. It will surface patterns, cite sources, ask questions, flag behaviours, and coach him toward his own decision. The trader is the decision-maker and the AI is the supervisor, and the product is built to make that boundary obvious in every piece of UI. The landing page must not blur this line. Every description of the copilot must use verbs of support, never verbs of instruction. Intercept, classify, flag, ask, surface, decompose, coach. Never decide, never recommend a trade, never tell you when to enter.

The Community Covenant.

No one can post a win without the system attaching the trade's full context — entry, exit, R, timeframe, session, whether a rule was broken. No one can DM a minor. No one can offer paid services inside a public room without the mentor flag. No one can run a challenge. No one can sell an indicator without publishing the code. The goal is not restriction; it is the removal of the asymmetric-information pressure that makes retail rooms feel like casinos. The page must show that the room is calm because the rules are clear.

The Archio Covenant.

The thing we promise back to the user, in exchange for his trust. We will not sell his data. We will not run ads against his trading. We will not make our money from his volume. We will not accept paid placement from mentors. We will not introduce partners we would not recommend to our own brothers. We will show our own founders' trades on the platform — wins, losses, tilt episodes included — so that nothing the system asks of the user is something it does not first ask of us.

“Four covenants. One page each. Written before the first user signed up.”

How the landing page carries all this without saying all of it.

Trust is carried by restraint. If the page does not over-promise, the reader does not need to see the full covenant to believe that one exists. The words we are willing to use tell the reader as much as the words we are willing to publish in a legal document. The design should use the restraint of the copy as a trust signal: the absence of exclamation points is a signal; the absence of testimonial sliders is a signal; the absence of a countdown timer is a signal. The reader who has been on this side of the industry for years will feel it in the first three seconds, and he is the reader we are writing for.

§
18 The First One Thousand

Who this page is really written for, at launch.

A landing page written for everyone is a landing page read by no one. The page is written for the first one thousand traders who will ever read it — because those thousand will set the culture of the platform for its next hundred thousand. If the page attracts the right thousand, the next ninety-nine thousand will arrive already shaped. If it attracts the wrong thousand, we will spend the following two years trying to remove them.

The profile.

He is between twenty-four and forty. He has been trading, seriously, for between eighteen months and six years. He has lost an amount of money that genuinely hurt him at least once and he is no longer telling his friends about his winners. He still has the scars of his worst trade accessible in conversation. He has paid, and regretted paying, for at least one course or signal group. He does not call himself a trader at parties yet. He works at it every morning before his day job or full-time from a quiet room in the flat he rents.

When he reads the landing page, he is not looking for permission to trade. He is looking for permission to trust again — the product, the community, his own discipline. The page is written to give him that permission honestly, by not asking for too much, too fast.

What he is not.

He is not a hobbyist. He is not new. He is not a YouTube viewer who watched a reel on "prop firm strategies." He is not someone who thinks of the market as a gambling venue. He is not anti-psychology. He is not anti-AI. He is not anti-mentor, but he is allergic to guru-coded aesthetics. He is not impressed by lambos, Bali rooftops, or green-candle backdrops.

The Reddit and the Discord where he already lives.

There is a canonical set of places on the internet where this man spends his mornings. Certain subreddits — the quiet ones, where posts are deleted for being promotional. Certain Discord servers — the invite-only ones with fewer than a thousand members, where a post is a paragraph, not a screenshot. A handful of X accounts with five thousand followers each who trade institutional size without saying so. He respects these places because they have, against all odds, stayed clean. Our landing page must read like something that was made by someone who has been in those rooms and, for his own reasons, has stopped expecting anyone else to build for them. If the page reads like that, he forwards it to three friends inside the hour. If it does not, he does not send it to anyone.

The tone of our acquisition.

We do not run paid acquisition on the landing page at launch. There is no budget for Meta ads. The first thousand arrive because the page was posted by a respected account, screenshotted by a thoughtful account, or forwarded by a friend whose taste they trust. The page is the ad. The page has to be embarrassable to send — in the positive sense. It has to make the sender look like someone with taste.

The second thousand and beyond.

The second thousand will come through mentors. The third through prop firms. The fourth through brokers who want their better clients to stay alive longer. The fifth through a feature in a major publication. By the time the twentieth thousand arrives, the page will have been redesigned twice, but the shape of this first version — the restraint, the density, the warmth of the grammar — will still be visible in every later version. Like the first flag of a country. You can always tell.

§
19 The Moat

Why this is difficult to copy, and why that shows in the design.

Every serious product has a question a serious reader asks in his head: "Why can't someone else just build this?" The landing page does not answer that question out loud — an answer out loud would sound defensive — but it has to be built by people who know the answer, because the answer shapes every choice on the page.

01 · Integrated emotional data.

Any team with six months and a funded seed round can build a charting front-end. Two teams can build a journaling app in a weekend. A well-staffed AI team can build a pattern classifier in a month. What no team can build quickly is the corpus of paired trades and trader narratives that lets a model learn the specific shape of tilt — because that corpus does not exist on the open internet and it does not exist inside a broker's data warehouse. It only gets built inside a platform where the trader types his own sentence next to his own trade. Every trader who joins Archio and writes one journal entry makes the system a little better for the next. The moat compounds. The landing page does not claim this, but the design carries the weight of it.

02 · Permission.

A broker cannot build this product because the broker has the wrong incentive — no serious trader believes the company making money from his volume is the company best placed to tell him to stop. A charting platform cannot build this product because it has spent fifteen years training its users to associate it with charts, not psychology. A prop firm cannot build this product because its business is selling challenges, not extending careers. The only team that can build this product is a team that has chosen, deliberately, not to pick up any of those easier business models. That is a moat made of restraint, not technology. It shows in the landing page as the things the page refuses to do.

03 · Taste.

There is a reason the great consumer products of the last twenty years — the ones that made categories rather than competed in them — all look like they were made by small teams with strong preferences. Taste is difficult to clone because it is an accumulation of ten thousand small choices, each of them arguable, and most of them impossible to defend in a spreadsheet. A competitor can copy our features within a year. He cannot copy the feeling of the footer. He cannot copy the particular absence of an exclamation point. He cannot copy the way our three demos sit on the page. He cannot, most of all, copy the fact that the page reads like it was written by a trader who was up at four in the morning, for someone else who was up at four in the morning. That is what we are selling.

04 · Ecosystem lock.

The Forge sits on top of the broker connectors we have wired. The Psychology OS sits on top of the behavioural data the Forge emits. The Dashboard sits on top of the narrative the Journal captures. The Network sits on top of the mentor covenants we have already collected. Each module makes the next module more valuable, and each is less interesting on its own than with its neighbours. A competitor entering the market from the side will have to rebuild all four simultaneously, and the person who tries that is not going to beat us; he is going to release a worse version of each of them and quietly pivot.

05 · First flag.

The first mover in a category does not always win, but the first mover who gets the category name right almost always does. "Trading OS" is the language we plant. Every competitor who arrives afterward will be measured against a phrase we wrote. The landing page is the document that plants that flag. Design accordingly.

“Taste is the only moat that does not erode. Everything else is a head start.”

§
20 Delivery & Cadence

Four phases. Clear ownership.

This brief does not specify a calendar, because calendars are a negotiation between us. It specifies the shape of the work. Four phases. Each one ends with a single artefact that we sign, named below. We expect a named delivery lead on QCLAY's side. We provide a named founder on ours.

  1. Phase 01 — Architecture. Sitemap, wireframes for the landing and every feature page, section weighting agreed. Artefact: a single PDF of greybox wireframes with our annotations approved. Owner: QCLAY lead. Reviewer: founders.
  2. Phase 02 — Surface. Visual design for the landing page and one feature page (we suggest Psychology OS, because it is the hardest). Full type, palette, motion language established. Artefact: two Figma files (landing + one feature page), fully specced, ready for engineering. Owner: QCLAY art direction. Reviewer: founders.
  3. Phase 03 — Extension. The remaining four feature pages (Network, Forecast, Forge, Dashboard AI), each brought to parity with the Psychology OS template. The Feel It demos are specced in motion prototypes. Artefact: five feature page Figmas + motion prototypes. Owner: QCLAY + founders co-driving copy. Reviewer: founders.
  4. Phase 04 — Fabrication. Engineering handoff. Every asset exported, every breakpoint specced, every interaction documented. Archio engineering builds. QCLAY stands by for QA on fidelity. Artefact: live staging URL, founder-signed. Owner: Archio engineering. Reviewer: QCLAY + founders.

What we sign off on, and when.

We sign off at four moments only: end of Phase 01 (architecture), end of Phase 02 (visual language), end of Phase 03 (extension parity), and end of Phase 04 (live). No design-by-committee. No WhatsApp revisions. Every sign-off is documented in a single paragraph we both initial, and that paragraph is the contract for the next phase. Change requests outside of these four gates are tracked as a separate scope.

How we work during the phases.

One call per week, thirty minutes, standing. One shared Notion workspace with live commenting. One WhatsApp thread for urgent clarifications — always answered within the business day. No group calls unless requested. No Slack. QCLAY's lead has our phone numbers. We have his.

§
22 Closing

The standard we are building toward.

"The best work of our generation will be the work that brings order to a place that accepted its chaos for too long. Retail finance is that place. The landing page is the first room of that order."

— ArchioAI, 2026

The number of companies that have ever tried to do what we are asking QCLAY to help us do is zero. There is no precedent we can point you to, no reference site we can ask you to outdo, no competitor whose landing we want to beat. The standard we are building toward is not a benchmark; it is an absence. We want this page to be the thing future teams point to when they want to show a designer what "order" looks like on the open internet.

When it is done, it should feel the way a great novel feels in the first paragraph — not clever, not salesy, not trying; just confident that the author knows something the reader is about to find out. It should be quiet, dense, warm, and absolutely sure of itself. A reader should be able to linger on any single section of it for a full minute and not run out of something to read. A skeptical reader should close the tab and come back the next day because he was not done.

We believe that, built correctly, this page will still be the canonical example of its category ten years from now. Not because we will have been unchanged — the product will have evolved a hundred times — but because the shape of this first room will have set the shape of every room that followed. Structure is the most valuable thing a young category can inherit, and structure is what this document is about.

“Bend the spec. Do not bend the feeling.”

— The only line we insist on

Thank you for reading. Thank you for taking this seriously. We know what this page is worth and what we are paying for it, and we know that a trivially smaller brief would have been easier to write. We chose this length because the work deserves it. We trust you to do the same.
